 Economic offences warrant greater scrutiny in anticipatory bail pleas: HC

 Jagpreet Singh / Nov 15, 2026, 00:18 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print Chandigarh: The Punjab and Haryana high court has held that courts must approach anticipatory bail pleas in economic offence cases with greater circumspection when allegations are backed by identifiable transactions and documentary evidence establishing a prima facie link with the accused. Justice Sumeet Goel made the observations while dismissing the anticipatory bail plea of Amlan Dutta, former vice-president of Trehan IRIS, in an alleged investment fraud involving more than Rs 7 crore. The court observed that economic offences are characterised by “calculated design, deliberation, sophistication and a conscious abuse of financial, commercial and fiduciary mechanisms”. It added, “Economic offence(s), though invariably not attended by physical violence, cannot on that account be regarded as less serious.” Elaborating on the principles governing anticipatory bail in such cases, the court said: “Where the accusation is founded upon identifiable transactions, documentary material, financial trails, communications, corporate records, statements, digital evidence or other contemporaneous material which, at the stage of consideration of anticipatory bail, prima facie attributes a definite and active role to the accused, the court would necessarily be required to approach the prayer for anticipatory bail with greater circumspection. ” The bench clarified that courts were not expected to conduct a detailed assessment of evidence at the anticipatory bail stage, but could not disregard material of substantial probative value indicating a direct link between the accused and the alleged offence. The case was registered at Sadar police station in Gurgaon on Aug 13, 2026, under sections 318(4) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The allegations arose from investments made by four complainants in the Omara and Iris Broadway projects of the Trehan IRIS group. According to the prosecution, Abhishek Kumar Gupta invested Rs 50 lakh, Suvendu Banerjee Rs 2.3 crore, Sanket Kaparia Rs 3.85 crore and Mohit Kumar Rs 70 lakh. They alleged that Dutta, claiming to be the company’s vice-president, assured them that the company would sell their investments and pay them the premium generated. Seeking anticipatory bail, Dutta argued that he had been falsely implicated and that the dispute was essentially commercial. His counsel submitted that he had acted on the instructions of the company’s authorities and that his personal bank account had been used by the company to route transactions and meet its liabilities. Opposing the plea, the state argued that Dutta had lured investors and received substantial amounts in his personal account. His custodial interrogation was necessary to recover the alleged proceeds, investigate cash transactions and establish the role of other accused, it submitted. Dismissing the plea, the high court noted that Dutta was the company’s vice-president when the investments were made and that the money had been credited to his personal bank account. It also noted his admission that the company had used his account to route transactions. Join conversation

 The bench further observed that Dutta had failed to produce WhatsApp instructions or supporting material to substantiate his claim that he had acted on the company’s directions. His admission of involvement in another FIR and his criminal antecedents were also relevant considerations, it said. “No plausible cause” had been shown at this stage to indicate false implication, the court held. “In view of the seriousness and gravity of the allegations, this court finds no compelling ground to extend the benefit of discretionary relief of anticipatory bail to the petitioner. Moreover, custodial interrogation of the petitioner is necessary for an effective investigation and to unravel the truth,” it added.
